paras: The death of an accused poisoner at Windsor, Missouri, took place on June 3, 1888, when a Black servant girl in the household of a Windsor man named Owsley died after drinking coffee she was accused of poisoning. A widely reprinted wire dispatch said she had been forced to drink the coffee and died within half an hour, while two Missouri dispatches said she tasted it at her mistress's word or drank it when accused of being afraid.

According to a dispatch from Clinton in the same county, R. N. Ousley, a 'well-known business man' of Windsor, had hired a 14-year-old Black girl to do housework and cooking, and she was 'chastised' but kept on after stealing clothes and selling them to gypsies. A Windsor dispatch printed in the Forrest City Times told it differently, saying she had given sugar and other small things to gypsies, who were arrested, and that Mr. and Mrs. Owsley 'corrected' her, which made her angry. The wire report added that John Owsley had fallen ill three days earlier and was found to have taken rat poison, and that the 12-year-old servant was suspected but denied it.

On the morning of June 3, members of the family fell sick at breakfast and the coffee came under suspicion. In the wire version, strychnine was found in the coffee and the girl, again denying guilt, refused to drink it; she was then forced to drink, by persons the dispatch did not name, and died in half an hour after confessing and naming other Black people who she said had made her do it. Only the San Antonio Daily Light's one-line summary said it was 'the family she had poisoned' that made her drink.

The Clinton dispatch described no force: her mistress told her to taste the coffee, after which she ran from the house, was overtaken a mile and a half away, brought back, and 'died instantly.' In the Forrest City Times account, Mrs. Owsley asked whether she had put something in the coffee and, when the girl would not drink it, accused her of being afraid; the girl said she was not, drank, and ran. Mr. Owsley set out after her but was too sick to keep up the chase; the account as preserved breaks off there.

Medical aid was summoned for the family, whose members were reported in critical condition and not expected to recover. No report of an inquest, of any arrest of the people the girl was said to have named, or of the family's later condition was found, and no paper gave the girl's name.

The wire story ran in the Washington Evening Star on June 4 and the New York Sun on June 5, then spread within a week to Kansas, South Carolina and, in German translation, the Illinois Staats-Zeitung. Its headlines stressed the forcing and her guilt: the Sun used 'Forced Her to Drink,' the Wheeling Register 'A Murder Plot Confessed,' and the Western Kansas World 'Caught in Her Own Trap.'

The Clinton version, headed 'A Young Fiend's Work' in the Butler Weekly Times, called her 'the faithless servant' and reached Kansas readers in the Abilene Reflector and the Iola Register under the line 'Her Own Death.' The Forrest City Times headed its account 'A Youthful Borgia' and opened with the family's narrow escape. None of these papers questioned the report that she had been forced to drink or treated her death as a matter for the law; they presented her as the poisoner and the family as the victims.

The accounts disagreed on whether she was compelled to drink: the wire said she was forced, the Clinton dispatch said her mistress told her to taste the coffee, and the Windsor account said she drank when challenged. They also differed on her age (12 or 14), the poison (strychnine or 'Rough on Rats') and the number poisoned (six or three); the two Missouri-datelined dispatches, both filed on June 3, are the nearer sources, and neither reports that anyone forced her to drink. The wire blamed other Black people she named, while the Clinton dispatch's headline called the cause 'spite.'

reader.title: Death of an accused poisoner at Windsor, Missouri
bases: A Black servant girl accused of poisoning her employer's family died after drinking the coffee, forced to by unnamed persons in the wire version (A2, A7) but tasting it at her mistress's word or on a dare in the Missouri dispatches (A6, A10); no mob or crowd is reported.

She died after drinking coffee she was accused of poisoning, and the wire report says she was forced to drink it (A2, A14), but it names no one who forced her and gives no number, while two Missouri dispatches say she drank it when told to taste it or when accused of being afraid (A6, A10). Whether she was killed by others, and by a group of three or more, cannot be settled from the coverage.
Independent dispatches agree that the girl died after drinking the coffee (A2, A6, A10), but they contradict one another on whether she was forced to drink it.

accounts.label: Wire report (Windsor via Chicago)
accounts.gist: After strychnine was found in the coffee, the girl denied guilt and refused to drink; she was forced to drink and died in half an hour, after confessing and naming Black people who she said made her do it.

accounts.label: Clinton, Mo., county dispatch
accounts.gist: Told by her mistress to taste the coffee, she did so, ran from the house, was overtaken a mile and a half away, brought back, and died instantly; the motive was spite over being chastised for theft.

accounts.label: Windsor dispatch (Forrest City Times)
accounts.gist: Accused by Mrs. Owsley of being afraid to drink the coffee, she said she was not, drank, and ran; Mr. Owsley was too sick to keep up the chase.

framing.detail: The wire story ran under headlines stressing the forcing and her guilt: 'Forced Her to Drink', 'A Murder Plot Confessed', 'Caught in Her Own Trap'.
The Butler Weekly Times headlined the Clinton dispatch 'A Young Fiend's Work' and called her 'the faithless servant', without describing any force against her.
The Forrest City Times headed its account 'A Youthful Borgia', centering the family's narrow escape.
The San Antonio Daily Light's brief called her 'a negro girl poisoner' forced to take 'her own decoction' by the family.
